title: WORLD OF DECISION
sub: July 1914: Could the war have been prevented?
hook: On 28 June 1914, shots rang out in Sarajevo. Thirty-seven days later, Europe was at war. Step into the shoes of a decision-maker in Germany, Austria-Hungary, Russia, France, Britain or Serbia, and live those 37 days again. Can you stop the war?
prologue: On the morning of Sunday, 28 June 1914, in Sarajevo, the capital of Bosnia, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the throne of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, and his wife Sophie were shot dead. The gunman was Gavrilo Princip, a nineteen-year-old Bosnian Serb, and the assassins had received weapons and help crossing the border through the Black Hand, a secret society led by Dragutin Dimitrijević, known as "Apis," the head of Serbian military intelligence. How much the Serbian government knew of the plot is still debated among historians.

Europe was then divided into two camps. On one side stood the Triple Alliance of Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy; on the other, the Triple Entente, in which Britain cooperated loosely with the alliance of France and Russia. Britain worked with France and Russia but had no treaty obligation to fight alongside them. Russia cast itself as the protector of Serbia, a fellow Slav nation.

In the days after the assassination, many in Europe saw it as no more than another Balkan tragedy. Yet five weeks later all five of Europe’s great powers except Italy would be at war. Now the decisions of those five weeks are yours to make.

A.title: A Summer Without War
A.text: In August 1914, Europe’s trains carried summer vacationers instead of soldiers. The Sarajevo affair was settled at the great powers' conference table, as the Balkan Wars of 1912–1913 had been. That did not mean the danger had passed. The alliance system, the arms race and the national conflicts within Austria-Hungary all remained. The historian Christopher Clark called the leaders of 1914 "sleepwalkers" who walked on without seeing what lay ahead. This time the leaders saw the danger in time and stepped back by negotiating.

B.title: The War That Stopped at Belgrade
B.text: The Austrian army took Belgrade and halted. Russia went no further than partial mobilization, and the great powers handed the Serbian question over to negotiation. It ended as a small Balkan war, but in Russia anger built up at having failed once again to protect its Slav brothers. Russia’s retreat in the Bosnian crisis of 1908–1909 was one of the reasons Russia’s leaders resolved in July 1914 never to back down again.

C.title: A War in the East Alone
C.text: Germany and Austria fought Russia, while France and Britain looked on. There were no trenches on a Western Front, no slaughter at Verdun or on the Somme. But in the east, too, the war was long and terrible. As it happened, the Russian Empire fell in the February Revolution of 1917, two and a half years into the war; had the war been fought only in the east, no one can say whether that moment would have come sooner or later.

D.title: A Continental War Without Britain
D.text: Britain stayed out of the war, and Germany fought France and Russia. In The Pity of War (1998), the historian Niall Ferguson made the controversial argument that had Britain not entered the war, Germany would have won quickly and an order would have emerged in which Germany dominated the European continent economically. Others counter that France and Russia, even without Britain, would have held out longer.

E.title: The World War, as It Happened
E.text: On the night of 4 August 1914, Britain declared war on Germany, and with that all five of Europe’s great powers except Italy were at war (Italy entered in 1915). Grey, the British foreign secretary, recorded in his memoirs that one evening just before Britain entered the war (on 3 August, as a friend remembered it), looking out of a window of the Foreign Office, he remarked: "The lamps are going out all over Europe; we shall not see them lit again in our life-time." The war that was to be over by Christmas lasted four years and three months.

F.title: The Great War Postponed
F.text: The crisis of 1914 passed, but when another crisis came a few years later, someone moved first. After several more years of the arms race, that war may well have been larger and more destructive still. Depending on the choices that follow, a decision that keeps the peace may do no more than buy time.

G.title: Peace by Submission
G.text: In the summer of 1914, Serbia did not take up arms. Austro-Hungarian officials joined the investigation on Serbian soil to hunt down those behind the assassination, and the great powers of Europe were relieved to have avoided a great war. But in return for accepting foreign officials in the investigation, Serbia had to surrender the dignity of an independent state and part of its sovereignty.

history: The dead: an estimated 15 to 20 million soldiers and civilians were killed (estimates vary).
The fall of empires: four empires collapsed, the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman. Revolution broke out in Russia in 1917.

The end, and the seeds of the next war: the armistice of 11 November 1918 and the Treaty of Versailles in 1919. The harsh peace terms imposed on defeated Germany became one of the causes of the Second World War twenty years later.

The debate over responsibility: the best-known works are Fritz Fischer’s 1961 study, which stressed Germany’s responsibility for the war, and Christopher Clark’s The Sleepwalkers (2012), which sees the misjudgments of many countries compounding one another.
eastasia: Invoking the Anglo-Japanese Alliance, Japan declared war on Germany on 23 August 1914 and in November captured Qingdao in China, the main city of Germany’s leased territory at Jiaozhou Bay.
In 1915 Japan presented China with the Twenty-One Demands and extracted concessions, among them the transfer of Germany’s rights in Shandong.

The principle of national self-determination that US President Wilson put forward in 1918, in his Fourteen Points (January) and an address to Congress (February), raised great hopes among colonized peoples. The New Korea Youth Party sent Kim Kyu-sik to the Paris Peace Conference in 1919, and the March First Movement broke out in Korea the same year.
But the Paris Peace Conference handed Germany’s rights in Shandong to Japan, and in protest China’s May Fourth Movement arose.

a: Most historians agree that Serbia rejected it with its eyes open. At 3 p.m. on 25 July, about three hours before handing over its reply, Serbia had already ordered general mobilization and was preparing to move the government to Niš.

Any investigation would have led back to the state itself. The assassins' bombs came from a Serbian state arsenal, those who helped them with weapons and the border crossing were Serbian army officers and officials, and above them stood Apis, head of the intelligence department of the General Staff. If Austrian officials took part in the investigation, these facts could come to light, along with whether the government had known of the plot in advance.

Domestic politics did not allow acceptance either. In 1903 army officers had murdered the king and queen in a coup; in the spring of 1914 the Pašić government and the officer corps clashed hard over who would govern the newly won territories; and a general election was due in August.

Foreign officials taking part in the investigation would also have violated Serbia’s constitution and its code of criminal procedure. Historians differ over whether news that Russia would stand behind Serbia hardened the refusal.

War with Serbia had all but been decided. At the joint council of ministers on 7 July, everyone except the Hungarian prime minister, Tisza, leaned toward military action; the ultimatum was designed from the start to be rejected; and Giesl, the minister in Belgrade, already had instructions to leave unless it was accepted unconditionally.

The anger did not come from Sarajevo alone. Vienna saw a threat to the very existence of its multinational empire in a long series of events: the arrival of a pro-Russian dynasty in 1903, the customs dispute that began in 1906 (the Pig War), the Bosnian annexation crisis of 1908–1909, and the great growth of Serbia’s territory and of the South Slav national movement after the two Balkan Wars.

In March 1909 Serbia had declared that it would live on good-neighborly terms with Austria-Hungary, but Vienna believed the promise had not been kept. Hence the demand that this time Austrian officials would supervise compliance in person.
What Vienna was after was a local war to punish Serbia. It calculated that with Germany behind it, Russia would back down as it had in 1909, but that calculation proved wrong.
